Eliab
ē-lī'ăb
n. (Jesse's firstborn, passed over at the anointing of David — the tall man God refused, and the elder brother who despised the shepherd)
From Hebrew 'Eli'ab, “God is father”, from 'El, God, and 'ab, father. Several men bear it, including the prince of Zebulun in the wilderness and a Reubenite whose sons were swallowed with Korah.

Biblical Definition

Eliab was the eldest of Jesse's eight sons — “Jesse begat his firstborn Eliab, and Abinadab the second, and Shimma the third” (1Ch 2:13) — and Scripture uses him twice to make the same point. When Samuel came to Bethlehem with the horn of oil, Eliab was brought first, and the prophet, who had spent a lifetime in the LORD's service, got it wrong on sight and said so. The answer given him is one of the most quoted verses in the Old Testament and one of the least believed: “Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1Sa 16:7). The second occasion is the valley of Elah, where Eliab, standing in an army that had not moved for forty days, turned on his youngest brother for asking a question: “Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart” (1Sa 17:28). It is a perfect specimen of the accusation that describes the accuser. Eliab is not, however, cast off: his daughter Abihail married Rehoboam (2Ch 11:18), so his blood entered the royal line after all.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Eliab; in sacred history it is the name of the eldest son of Jesse, of a prince of Zebulun, and of a Reubenite in the time of Moses.

ELIAB, n. A Hebrew name signifying God is father.

The eldest son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, and brother of David.

Samuel, seeing him, thought the Lord's anointed was before him, but the Lord refused him.

He served in the army of Saul, and was angry with David in the valley of Elah.

Eliab the son of Helon was prince of the tribe of Zebulun in the wilderness.

Key Scripture

1Ch 2:13 — "And Jesse begat his firstborn Eliab, and Abinadab the second, and Shimma the third,"

1Sa 16:7 — "But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."

1Sa 17:28 — "And Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spake unto the men; and Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle."

2Ch 11:18 — "And Rehoboam took him Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David to wife, and Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse;"

Modern Corruption

1Sa 16:7 is used to license indifference about outward conduct — God sees the heart, so the visible does not matter; the verse is about God's power to see what man cannot, not about the irrelevance of what man can.

expand to see more

“Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” is regularly deployed to mean that God is unconcerned with how a professing Christian looks, speaks, dresses, or behaves in public. That is a use the verse cannot bear. The point of contrast is not appearance versus reality but human blindness versus divine sight: Samuel could see a tall man and could not see a heart, and God could. Far from making the outward indifferent, Scripture insists that the heart eventually shows — “by their fruits ye shall know them” (Mat 7:20), and “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh” (Mat 12:34). Eliab proved the diagnosis himself one chapter later, when the heart God had already refused came out of his mouth in the valley of Elah.

The second corruption is the flattening of Eliab into a mere foil. He was a soldier in a paralysed army, watching a giant blaspheme every morning for six weeks, and no doubt hating himself for it — and then his little brother arrived, asked what the reward was, and made everyone uncomfortable. His accusation, “I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart”, is a projection so exact that it functions as a confession. The temptation is a common one in the church: the man who will not act resents the man who does, and dresses the resentment as discernment about the other man's motives. David's reply is the model — “Is there not a cause?” — and then he turned away from him to someone else and got on with it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Eli'ab (H446), from 'El (H410), God, and 'ab (H1), father; ra'ah (H7200), to see; lebab (H3824), the heart.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Eli'ab (H446) — Eliab, “God is father”; borne by Jesse's firstborn and others.

Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, to look at; used three times in 1Sa 16:7, of man's sight and God's.

Hebrew 'enayim — the eyes; the Hebrew of “outward appearance” is literally “to the eyes”.

Hebrew lebab (H3824) — the heart; in Hebrew the seat of mind, will, and affection together, not the emotions alone.

Hebrew ma'as (H3988) — to reject, refuse; “I have refused him”, the same verb used of Saul in 1Sa 15:23.

Usage

"“Jesse begat his firstborn Eliab” — the son everyone would have chosen."

"“The LORD looketh on the heart” — the reason he was passed by."

"“I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart” — an accusation that named its author."
